summary_responses.response: Treasury proposes a new Privacy Act system of records to support its oversight and management of the federal student aid portfolio. The Department of Education will share personally identifiable and other data on Title IV grant recipients and student loan borrowers from systems including NSLDS, DMCS, and EDMAPS. Treasury plans to use the information for portfolio administration, research, policy analysis, monitoring, reporting, compliance, audits, and data-quality reviews under an interagency agreement. Education will remain the authoritative custodian of its program records, while Treasury says it will protect shared information under applicable privacy and security laws, including FERPA, using access controls and other safeguards. The Treasury Department issued a final rule updating its auction regulations for marketable Treasury bills, notes, and bonds to support an upcoming auction-system upgrade and clarify current terminology.  
The changes revise definitions and examples, remove outdated references, and align auction rules and announcements, without changing inflation-protected securities’ calculations.  
Submitters must provide each noncompetitive customer’s name and bid amount before the noncompetitive auction closes; summary bid amounts will no longer be permitted.  
Treasury also updated rules on auction awards and clarified that auction results will be posted on its website without specifying a particular web address.  
Most changes take effect October 15, 2026, while changes to customer-bid and auction-award provisions apply starting with the first auction using the upgraded system.

key_fact_breakdown.key_fact: The Department of the Treasury issued final amendments to 31 CFR Part 356 (the Uniform Offering Circular for Treasury Bills, Notes, and Bonds) with an effective date of October 15, 2026.

The amendments modify requirements for submitting noncompetitive customer bids to require submitters to provide each individual customer's name and bid amount prior to the noncompetitive auction close, eliminating the ability to submit summary bid amounts.

The changes to 31 CFR 356.14 and 356.23 apply to auctions beginning with the first Treasury marketable securities auction conducted using Treasury's upgraded auction system, which will be communicated to market participants in advance.

The final rule is exempt from Administrative Procedure Act notice and comment requirements under 5 U.S.C. 553(a)(2) because the auction regulations relate to Treasury securities, which are contracts between Treasury and the security owner.

The amendments update terminology throughout the UOC to align with Treasury's current auction terminology, including using 'award' and 'recognize' in lieu of 'accept' and 'tender' in sections 356.20 and 356.23.
Outdated references, such as to paper bids and the former CUSIP issuer, were removed from 31 CFR Part 356.

summary_responses.response: The paper introduces DiffTry, a method that gives higher-priority microservice requests more retry attempts than lower-priority requests. By applying different retry limits locally, it prioritizes valuable traffic and curbs retry storms without overload detection, service coordination, or application changes. The authors develop analytical models for individual services and larger networks to estimate class-specific rejection and completion rates, and prove convergence and monotonicity properties. Simulations show the models are accurate, while network analysis suggests the prioritization can hold across downstream services. A live Kubernetes deployment using a service-mesh plugin closely matched the predictions, supporting DiffTry’s practical effectiveness.

key_fact_breakdown.key_fact: DiffTry (Differential Retries) is a stateless mechanism that assigns different retry-attempt limits to different priority classes of requests to achieve differentiation in rejection rates.
Under overload with DiffTry, high-priority requests achieve a rejection rate of around 15% and account for about 85% of successful completions when both classes contribute 50% of input load.
DiffTry requires neither overload sensing nor microservices coordination and is implemented as a drop-in service-mesh plugin requiring no application code changes.

The paper develops an analytical model for DiffTry starting with two services in tandem, then generalizes it to networks of services using an open-network model combined with flow classes and priorities.

summary_responses.response: The FAA has adopted a new airworthiness directive, effective November 18, 2026, for certain Bombardier BD-700-2A12 airplanes. Low clearances among fuel, hydraulic, and vent components in the right wing could create an ignition source in a fuel tank if struck by lightning. The directive requires correcting specified clearances, inspecting the hydraulic lines and fuel vent tube, and replacing support brackets if inspection finds inadequate clearance, following Transport Canada’s directive. The FAA found the prescribed compliance measures adequate and said an emergency directive, shorter deadline, or interim operating restrictions were not necessary; it also said the condition would not cause fuel starvation. For 60 U.S.-registered airplanes, required work is estimated at $2,693 per aircraft, with an additional $5,772 per aircraft if bracket replacement is needed.

The AD was prompted by Transport Canada AD CF-2025-49 dated October 1, 2025, which reported low clearance conditions in the right wing between fuel line flexible coupling and harness support bracket clip-nut, between fuel line flexible coupling and hydraulic system, and between hydraulic system and fuel vent tube.

summary_responses.subtopic: Public Administration, Labor Policy & Family Leave
summary_responses.response: OPM’s direct final rule updates its Family and Medical Leave Act regulations to reflect statutory amendments enacted in 2021 and 2023. Nearly all qualifying federal civilian service—including temporary or intermittent service—may count toward the 12-month eligibility requirement, as may honorable active service in the Army, Navy, Air Force, Space Force, or Marine Corps. However, counting such service toward the requirement does not by itself make temporary or intermittent employees eligible to use title 5 FMLA leave. The rule confirms that qualifying annual or sick leave provided under non-title 5 authorities may be substituted for unpaid FMLA leave and excludes certain Veterans Health Administration employees from title 5 FMLA coverage. These changes also affect paid parental leave eligibility; the rule takes effect December 14, 2026, unless OPM receives significant adverse comments by November 16, 2026.

key_fact_breakdown.key_fact: The Office of Personnel Management is issuing a direct final rule making technical revisions to OPM's Family and Medical Leave Act (FMLA) regulations to incorporate statutory amendments from January 2021 and December 2023.
The rule is effective December 14, 2026, unless significant adverse comments are received by November 16, 2026.
The statutory changes make virtually all Federal civilian service and certain honorable active military service qualify for determining FMLA eligibility.
The rule excludes certain Veterans Health Administration (VHA) employees covered by a leave system under 38 U.S.C. 7421 from title 5 FMLA coverage.

The December 2023 amendment allows honorable active service in the Army, Navy, Air Force, Space Force, or Marine Corps to count toward the 12-month service requirement for FMLA eligibility, but does not include service in the Coast Guard or commissioned corps of the Public Health Service.
The minimum qualifying service for FMLA eligibility under title 5 is 12 months.
